[[Washington State Cougars football|Washington State]] (1991–1992) | undraftedyear = 1993 | pastteams = * [[Atlanta Falcons]] ({{NFL Year|1993|1999}}) * [[Seattle Seahawks]] ({{NFL Year|2000|2006}}) | highlights = * [[Pro Bowl]] ([[2006 Pro Bowl|2005]]) * [[Seattle Seahawks#35th Anniversary Team (2010)|Seattle Seahawks 35th Anniversary team]] * [[Seattle Seahawks#Top 50 Players (2025)|Seattle Seahawks Top 50 players]] * Second-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference football teams|All-Pac-10]] ([[1992 All-Pacific-10 Conference football team|1992]]) | statlabel1 = Games played | statvalue1 = 176 | statlabel2 = Games started | statvalue2 = 166 | statlabel3 = [[Fumble|Fumble recoveries]] | statvalue3 = 4 | statlabel4 = [[Reception (American football)|Reception]]s | statvalue4 = 2 | statlabel5 = [[Receiving yards]] | statvalue5 = 15 | statlabel6 = [[Touchdown|Receiving touchdowns]] | statvalue6 = 1 | pfr = TobeRo55 }} '''Robert Lee Tobeck'''{{Cite web |title=Robbie Tobeck Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TobeRo55.htm |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|t|oʊ|b|ɛ|k}}; born March 6, 1970) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[center (American football)|center]] for fourteen seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). Tobeck played seven seasons for the [[Seattle Seahawks]] after being acquired as a [[free agent]] from the [[Atlanta Falcons]] after signing as a [[rookie]] in 1993. Tobeck started his [[College football|college career]] after accepting a [[scholarship]] to [[Liberty University]] in [[Lynchburg, Virginia]], but was [[redshirted]] as a freshman. He transferred to [[Kilgore College]], a [[junior college]] in [[Kilgore, Texas]] for two years (1989–90) and then went on to play big league college football for the [[Washington State Cougars football|Washington State Cougars]]. During high school, Tobeck attended [[New Port Richey]] (FL) Christian, which, until his senior year, only offered a [[flag football]] program. He only played four games of tackle football in High school. However, the [[basketball]] program was a standout and Tobeck was a major part of its program. Tobeck retired at the end of the [[2006 NFL season]], on January 15, 2007, after a playoff loss to the [[Chicago Bears]].{{Cite web |date=2007-01-15 |title=Seahawks center Tobeck, out since midseason, retires |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2731726 |access-date=2025-08-29 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press |language=en}} He played in two Super Bowls, [[Super Bowl XXXIII]] as a member of the Falcons and [[Super Bowl XL]] as a member of the Seahawks. Tobeck also made the NFC Pro Bowl Team in 2005.{{Cite web |title=2005 NFL Pro Bowlers |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2005/probowl.htm |access-date=2023-12-29 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} After football, Tobeck went into the insurance business and now co-owns Griffin MacLean Insurance Brokers. Tobeck has also dabbled in radio in his time since playing as a co-host of The Outdoor Line radio show, although he is no longer with the show.

'''Robert Eugene Abraham''' (born July 13, 1960) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] who played [[college football]] for North Carolina State.<ref>{{cite news |title=Robert Abraham mistaken for Gamecocks' Rogers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/centre-daily-times-robert-abraham-mistak/128671525/ |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[Centre Daily Times]] |date=7 November 1980 |page=16 |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author1=Bob Lipper |title=Abraham watching, waiting for Redden |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/richmond-times-dispatch-abraham-watching/128671667/ |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[Richmond Times-Dispatch]] |date=2 September 1981 |pages=D1, D3 |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |author1=Bill Woodward |title=Pride at steak for Wolfpack |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-news-and-observer-pride-at-steak-for/128671798/ |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[The News & Observer]] |date=22 April 1981 |page=12 |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{open access}}</ref> He was selected by the [[History of the Tennessee Titans|Houston Oilers]] in the third round of the [[1982 NFL draft]] with the 77th overall pick. He played there until 1988, mostly as a starter.<ref>{{Cite web |title=1982 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1982/draft.htm |access-date=2024-12-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> His best season came in 1984 when he started 16 games and had 106 solo tackles and 92 assists. He missed most of his final season with the team due to injuries.<ref>{{cite news |author1=Ernie Trubiano |title=Oiler's Abraham an inspiration for hometown kids |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-state-oilers-abraham-an-inspiration/128671911/ |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[The State (newspaper)|The State]] |date=6 June 1986 |page=D1 |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{open access}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=A tale of two Oilers linebackers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/abilene-reporter-news-a-tale-of-two-oile/128672358/ |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[Abilene Reporter-News]] |date=7 January 1988 |page=4C |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{open access}}</ref> He was waived by the Oilers in March 1988 but signed with the [[New York Giants]] shortly later.<ref>{{cite news |title=Giants acquire linebacker Abraham on waivers |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/asbury-park-press-giants-acquire-linebac/128672608/ |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[Asbury Park Press]] |agency=[[Associated Press]] |date=8 March 1988 |page=C2 |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{open access}}</ref> However, he was waived by the Giants in August the same year prior to the start of the season.<ref>{{cite news |author1=George Willis |title=Parcells ponders moving Johnson to Banks' sport |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/705093359/?terms=%22Robert%20Abraham%22&match=1 |access-date=22 July 2023 |work=[[Newsday]] |date=23 August 1988 |page=97 |quote=''Free agents Keith Davis and Robert Abraham were among the 10 players waived yesterday to trim the Giants' roster to 58.'' |via=[[Ancestry.com]]}}{{closed access}}</ref>

Waldrop''' (born December 1, 1971) is an American former professional [[gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[defensive tackle]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) and [[Canadian Football League]] (CFL). Waldrop played professionally for the NFL's [[Kansas City Chiefs]], and the [[Memphis Mad Dogs]] and [[Toronto Argonauts]] of the CFL.  He is a member of the [[College Football Hall of Fame]].

'''Robbert Lee Riddick''' (born April 26, 1957) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] for the [[Buffalo Bills]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Millersville Marauders]] as a running back and [[defensive back]]. He set numerous of the school's records in football as well as track and field. Riddick was selected by the Bills in the ninth round, 241st overall, of the [[1981 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1981 Buffalo Bills Draftees |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/buf/1981_draft.htm |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |date=1981-04-30 |title=Courier express. (Buffalo, N.Y.) 1964-1982, April 30, 1981, Image 12 |url=https://nyshistoricnewspapers.org/lccn/sn88074337/1981-04-30/ed-1/seq-12/ |language=en |issue=1981/04/30 |pages=12}}</ref>

Riddick played six seasons for the Bills. He started eight games and ran for 632 total yards in [[1986 Buffalo Bills season|1986]], and he became a short-yardage specialist in [[1988 Buffalo Bills season|1988]]. He sat out the 1982 and 1985 seasons after sustaining injuries to his right knee during training camp.<ref>{{Cite web |title=RIDDICK WANTS TO SHUFFLE FOR BUFFALO PRO FOOTBALL |url=https://www.mcall.com/news/mc-xpm-1986-09-06-2535545-story.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=The Morning Call|date=September 6, 1986 }}</ref>

Riddick's first 100-yard rushing game<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robb Riddick 1986 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RiddRo00.htm |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> of his career helped Hall of Fame coach [[Marv Levy]] record his first win as the Bills new coach on November 9, 1986.<ref>{{Cite web |last=DeLuca |first=Dave |title=30 years ago today: Marv Levy wins first game |url=https://buffalonews.com/sports/bills/30-years-ago-today-marv-levy-wins-first-game/article_ec18ff81-d4e5-5c66-a1e7-ac3d09aa5f7e.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Buffalo News |date=November 8, 2016 |language=en}}</ref>

Because of his high-jumping ability, Riddick became a short-yardage weapon for the Bills in 1988. He scored 12 rushing touchdowns,<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robb Riddick 1988 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RiddRo00.htm |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> all but three of which were from the opponent's 1-yard line; the longest of his rushing touchdowns was five yards. He added one TD reception and a blocked punt returned for a touchdown in the regular season plus one rushing TD in the Bills' playoff win over the Houston Oilers in the 1988 AFC Divisional Playoff Game to total 15 TDs<ref>{{Cite web |title=Robb Riddick Career Touchdown Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/R/RiddRo00.htm |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |title=Robb Riddick 15 TDs 1988 | date=April 18, 2015 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3mIfyVJg-O0 |language=en |access-date=2022-08-17}}</ref> that year, his final season of his NFL career.

He suffered what turned out to be a career-ending knee injury in the 1989 preseason finale against the Atlanta Falcons.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Carucci |first=Vic |title=RIDDICK'S SEASON ENDED BY INJURY; KNEE TENDON TORN |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/riddicks-season-ended-by-injury-knee-tendon-torn/article_7a264121-0dc0-5ac5-9491-f8abd4b55ef1.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Buffalo News |date=September 3, 1989 |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Carucci |first=Vic |title=RIDDICK RETIRES |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/riddick-retires/article_848d093d-8f33-5d3e-98cb-939a71d8e1dd.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Buffalo News |date=March 7, 1991 |language=en}}</ref>

Riddick's oldest son, Ian Riddick, played [[defensive back]] at the [[University of Pittsburgh]]. His youngest son, Andre Riddick, played for Ohio State University. His daughter, Gabrielle Riddick, is a high academic achiever and plays the upright bass. {{citation needed|date=November 2017}}

Before attending Millersville, Riddick went to Pennridge High School, where he was an outstanding football player. Riddick is from an accomplished family of other professional football players. His brother is former NFL safety and current ESPN broadcaster [[Louis Riddick]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=March 7, 2017 |title=Brothers who played pro football. |url=https://www.profootballhof.com/pfhof/media/Assets/Brothers_Mar_09_2017.pdf?ext=.pdf}}</ref> His cousins, [[Will Lewis (American football)|Will Lewis]] and [[Tim Lewis]], also played in the NFL and currently hold management positions for professional football teams.

He struggled with financial problems after retiring from the NFL.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Warner |first=Gene |title=RIDDICK HIT HARD BY REALITY AFTER GLORY DAYS END FORMER BILLS RUNNING BACK UPBEAT AS HE TACKLES DEBTS |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/riddick-hit-hard-by-reality-after-glory-days-end-former-bills-running-back-upbeat-as/article_03809443-3134-5770-97e6-ee87e6d68bd6.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Buffalo News |date=November 17, 1991 |language=en}}</ref> In 1994, unemployed and facing debt of $340,000, he filed bankruptcy.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Herbeck |first=Dan |title=EX-RUNNING BACK FOR THE BILLS FILES FOR BANKRUPTCY RIDDICK OWES CREDITORS $340,000 |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/ex-running-back-for-the-bills-files-for-bankruptcy-riddick-owes-creditors-340-000/article_24eaaa35-c614-58c5-9300-7c6d69831a6e.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Buffalo News |date=August 2, 1994 |language=en}}</ref>

As of 2020, Riddick worked in Atlanta as a fitness instructor.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Herbeck |first=Dan |title=Trooper was last person seen with woman who vanished in 1985, police say |url=https://buffalonews.com/news/local/trooper-was-last-person-seen-with-woman-who-vanished-in-1985-police-say/article_b226ae35-9eb5-5afa-8c9d-64ed07491fc5.html |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Buffalo News |date=January 24, 2020 |language=en}}</ref>

In 2021, he was named to the first class of Millersville University's Wall of Honor.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Millersville football announces plans for wall of honor, recognizes first class of honorees |url=https://millersvilleathletics.com/news/2021/2/9/millersville-football-announces-plans-for-wall-of-honor-recognizes-first-class-of-honorees.aspx |access-date=2022-08-17 |website=Millersville |language=en}}</ref>
